Phase-filed modeling is performed assuming a double-well free energy function with a minimum at φ = 0 and φ = 1 and a maximum at φ = ½.⁸ To determine how φ evolves to equilibrium, the code solves the Cahn-Hilliard equation:
dφ/dt = ∇·(M(φ)∇ dF/dφ) (Eqn.1)
M is the mobility and F is called the free-energy functional. The free energy functional needed to solve the Cahn-Hilliard equation (Eqn. 1) is:
F = ∫Ω [f(φ) + 1/2 ε² |∇φ|² + We] dΩ (Eqn. 2)
and the variational derivative of the free energy functional with elastic strain energy now becomes:
∂F/∂φ = ∂f/∂φ + ∂We/∂φ - ε²∇²φ (Eqn. 3)

where Ω is a volume of space, the function f(φ) is the double well potential, and ε is called the gradient energy coefficient (discussed in Section IV). The interfacial energy γ is proportional to ε. We is the elastic strain energy density which occurs due to a lattice misfit between the substrate and the film. Equation 1 can now be solved using an explicit finite difference method and applied across a three dimensional grid of points. It is necessary that the grip point spacing is small enough for accuracy and that the timestep is small so that the numerical method is stable.

If Equation 1 is solved analytically in 1D, one of the steady-state solutions, besides φ = 0, φ = ½, and φ = 1, is a tangent function. Thus it is possible for the two phase system to reach a stable equilibrium with diffuse interfaces separating the phases. The value of φ changes smoothly from 0 to 1 over the finite width of these diffuse interfaces. In order to produce pictures of the evolution for analysis, the system is contoured at φ = ½ , the value of φ that occurs at the middle of an interface.

To evolve the system, a forward Euler difference method is used. Although not as fast as other techniques because it requires a very small time step to maintain stability, the method is simple to implement and only the current state needs to be known in order to calculate states in the future (hence a “forward” method). The basic assumption of the Euler method is that all the terms beyond the 1st in the Taylor expansion of the function can be ignored over small time increments.
The forward Euler differencing equation is thus:
dφ(t)/dt ≈ (φ(t +Δt) - φ(t))/Δt (Eqn. 4)
III. Quantum Dot Simulations with Isotropic Interfacial Energy

The three-dimensional growth simulation developed in the project is a modified version of a two-dimensional simulation that was written by J.J. Eggleston.⁹ To simulate isotropic quantum dot growth, the free-energy functional F (Eqn. 1) can be rewritten by defining the free energy density of the material as a function of φ. Upon making the substitution for f(φ), Equation 1 can be rewritten as:
dφ/dt = ∇·[M∇{1/2 W (2φ³ - 3φ² + φ) - ε²∇²φ + ∂We/∂φ}] (Eqn. 5)

Thus an Euler method with a small enough time step can be used to calculate the phase value at each point in the future from the current phase values. The forward Euler method approximation (Eqn. 4) is combined with Equation 5 to produce an equation which can be solved on a computer using finite time steps to find φ:
(φ(t +Δt) - φ(t))/Δt = ∇·[M∇{1/2 W (2φ³ - 3φ² + φ) - ε²∇²φ + ∂We/∂φ}]|t (Eqn. 6)

Although the basic Equations which control the evolution of φ still apply in three dimensions, several changes had to be made to the two-dimensional code. First, two dimensional variables were give a third dimension. Initial boundary conditions had to be set in the new z-dimension, and the initial phasefield configuration had to be adapted to the new axis so that initial starting conditions could be configured. Laplacians and divergences had to be recalculated as follows, which requires the additional calculation of the derivative of φ in the z- direction, φz:
∇·φ = (φi+1,j,k - φi-1,j,k)/h + (φi,j+1,k - φi,j-1,k)/h + (φi,j,k+1 - φi,j,k-1)/h (Eqn. 7)
(∇²φ)i,j,k = (φi+1,j,k + φi-1,j,k + φi,j+1,k + φi,j-1,k + φi,j,k+1 + φi,j,k-1 - 6φi,j,k)/h² (Eqn. 8)
The simulation accounts for the elastic energy caused by atomic misfit between the film and the substrate.
